When latency rises but pods are Running/Ready, endpoints are populated, restarts are zero, and only the target pod's inbound/outbound call latency is elevated while peer pods and downstream dependencies stay normal, suspect pod_network_delay.
Distinguish it from CPU throttling/resource saturation by checking CFS throttling, memory, GC, and node pressure; from downstream/DB latency by tracing dependency spans and backend metrics; from service-wide/node-wide network issues by testing peers on the same node/namespace.
Rule out application exceptions, probe failures, endpoint churn, and downstream saturation before concluding; confirm with per-pod latency isolation and correlation to the fault window.
Prefer pod-level network fault evidence over aggregate service latency alerts alone, since propagated caller latency is a symptom, not the root cause.

#!/bin/bash

# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables in an unquoted
# assignment slot, then reference them only as "$VAR". Never interpolate
#  inside a quoted context - sanitize() (shlex.quote) wraps
# dangerous values in single quotes, which are literal (and command
# substitution stays active) inside a double-quoted or single-quoted slot.
KIND=events
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=tiktok-k8s-lab
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""

# Collapse multi-line jq expressions (LLMs sometimes write multi-line jq)
# Note: use $'\n' syntax instead of '\n' because Jinja2 interprets \n as literal newlines
JQ_FILTER='.items | sort_by(.lastTimestamp) | .[] | {t: .lastTimestamp, type: .type, reason: .reason, obj: .involvedObject.name, msg: .message}'
JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

}

# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints

  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."

# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a

#!/bin/bash
# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables (unquoted slot),
# then reference them only as "$VAR" - never interpolate 
# inside a quoted context. See kubernetes_jq_query for the rationale.
KIND=
CUSTOM_COLUMNS=
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
FILTER_PATTERN=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""
[ "$FILTER_PATTERN" = "None" ] && FILTER_PATTERN=""

# kubectl ignores -n for cluster-scoped kinds; say so instead of reporting a namespace that wasn't applied
NOTES='[]'
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  is_kind() { awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind || index($1, kind ".") == 1 {found = 1} END {exit !found}'; }
  if kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind \
    && ! kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind; then
    NOTES=$(jq -nc --arg note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${KIND} is cluster-scoped." '[$note]')
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
fi

SCOPE_ARGS=()
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-n "$SEL_NAMESPACE")
else
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--all-namespaces)
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-l "$SEL_LABELS")
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--field-selector "$SEL_FIELDS")
fi

err_file=$(mktemp)
output=$(kubectl get "$KIND" "${SCOPE_ARGS[@]}" -o custom-columns="$CUSTOM_COLUMNS" 2>"$err_file")
kubectl_exit=$?
err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

SCOPE='null'
if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
    '{namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
      label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
      field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')
fi

if [ $kubectl_exit -ne 0 ] || [ -z "$output" ]; then
  if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
    jq -n --arg stderr "$err_content" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
      '{count: 0, header: null, rows: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  else
    echo "=== STDERR ==="
    echo "$err_content"
    echo "=== ROWS ==="
    echo "=== COUNT ==="
    echo 0
  fi
  exit 0
fi

# Split header and data rows
header=$(echo "$output" | head -1)
if [ -n "$FILTER_PATTERN" ]; then
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2 | grep -E -- "$FILTER_PATTERN" || true)
else
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2)
fi

if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then
    count=$(echo "$data" | wc -l)
  else
    count=0
  fi
  # Rows go through stdin, not --argjson, so large tables don't hit "Argument list too long"
  printf '%s' "$data" | jq -R . | jq -s \
    --argjson count "$count" \
    --arg header "$header" \
    --arg stderr "$err_content" \
    --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
    '{count: $count, header: $header, rows: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
else
  echo "=== STDERR ==="
  echo "$err_content"
  echo "=== HEADER ==="
  echo "$header"
  echo "=== ROWS ==="
  echo "$data"
  echo "=== COUNT ==="
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then echo "$data" | wc -l; else echo 0; fi
fi

  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  exit 0
}

# The namespace becomes part of the raw API path, so anything other than a valid
# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."
fi

# Get the API path for the resource kind using kubectl
# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a
# grep regex - otherwise a kind like '.*' or 'a|b' would match the
# wrong resource.
CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)
# `kubectl api-resources` sorts by group name, so a CRD reusing a built-in
# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -c .)" -gt 1 ] && [[ "$API_INFO" != *" v1 "* ]]; then
  API_GROUPS=$(kubectl get --raw /apis 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.groups[].name' 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -z "$API_GROUPS" ]; then
    add_note "Several API groups serve '${KIND}' and server discovery (/apis) failed, so the first group listed by kubectl api-resources was used."
  fi
  for group in $API_GROUPS; do
    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)
    if [ -n "$match" ]; then
      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done
fi

if [ -z "$API_INFO" ]; then
  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Extract NAMESPACED value
if [[ "$API_INFO" == *" true "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."
fi

# Trim trailing spaces from prefix and collapse internal spaces
PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do
  ((FIELD_COUNT++))
done

RESOURCE_NAME="${PREFIX_FIELDS[0]}"
if [ $FIELD_COUNT -ge 2 ]; then
  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

if [ -z "$API_VERSION" ] || [ -z "$RESOURCE_NAME" ]; then
  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Build API path: namespaced kinds can be listed within one namespace;
# cluster-scoped kinds ignore the namespace (as kubectl does)
if [[ "$API_VERSION" == "v1" ]]; then
  API_BASE="/api/v1"
else
  API_BASE="/apis/${API_VERSION}"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && [ "$NAMESPACED" = "true" ]; then
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/namespaces/${SEL_NAMESPACE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
else
  if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
    add_note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${RESOURCE_NAME} is cluster-scoped."
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

SELECTOR_QUERY=""
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&labelSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_LABELS")"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&fieldSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_FIELDS")"
fi

SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg resource "$RESOURCE_NAME" --arg api_version "$API_VERSION" \
  --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
  '{resource: $resource, api_version: $api_version,
    namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
    label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
    field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')

# Process resources in chunks using API pagination
LIMIT=500
CONTINUE=""
TOTAL_MATCHES=0
ALL_MATCHES=""

while true; do
  QUERY="${API_PATH}?limit=${LIMIT}${SELECTOR_QUERY}"
  if [ -n "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    # continue tokens are base64 and may contain '+', '/' or '='
    QUERY="${QUERY}&continue=$(uri_encode "$CONTINUE")"
  fi

  OUTPUT=$(kubectl get --raw "$QUERY" 2>>"$err_file")
  exit_code=$?

  if [ $exit_code -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "kubectl get --raw failed for $QUERY."
  fi

  ITEMS_COUNT=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq '.items | length')

  MATCHES=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -c "$JQ_FILTER" 2>>"$err_file")
  jq_exit=$?
  if [ $jq_exit -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "jq expression failed."
  fi

  if [ "$ITEMS_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
    if [ -n "$MATCHES" ]; then
      if [ -z "$ALL_MATCHES" ]; then
        ALL_MATCHES="$MATCHES"
      else
        ALL_MATCHES="$ALL_MATCHES"$'\n'"$MATCHES"
      fi
      MATCH_COUNT=$(echo "$MATCHES" | grep -c . || true)
      TOTAL_MATCHES=$((TOTAL_MATCHES + MATCH_COUNT))
    fi
    PROCESSED=$((PROCESSED + ITEMS_COUNT))
  fi

  CONTINUE=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -r '.metadata.continue // empty')

  if [ -z "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    break
  fi
done

err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

# Output results as a JSON object with metadata. Results go through stdin, not --argjson:
# Linux caps a single argument at 128KB, so larger results failed with "Argument list too long".
printf '%s\n' "$ALL_MATCHES" | jq -s \
  --argjson total_items_processed "$PROCESSED" \
  --argjson matches_found "$TOTAL_MATCHES" \
  --arg stderr "$err_content" \
  --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
  --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
  '{total_items_processed: $total_items_processed, matches_found: $matches_found, results: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

I found a skill named **Pod-Scoped Network Delay Diagnosis for Service Latency Degradation**（note-02）and used it to troubleshoot:

1. ✅ *确认 Pod 运行态/就绪态、重启数、Endpoints* — `api-6c9b55d878-6w9mt` / `api-6c9b55d878-tvc5g` 均 Running/Ready，restart=0；`redis-0` Running（历史 restart=1，是 11-11 15:17 的 SIGTERM 重启，非本次）；`api`/`redis`/`redis-headless` 的 Endpoints 均正常有地址。
2. ✅ *排除探针失败、Endpoint 抖动、应用异常* — 近 1h 事件仅 14 条（Scheduled/Pulled/Created/Started/SuccessfulCreate/Killing/SuccessfulDelete，属 13:07:51–13:08:33 的正常滚动更新），无 probe failed/BackOff；api 日志中 `error|timeout|warn|throttl|oom|retry|fail` 命中 0 条，所有 POST /events 均返回 202。
3. ✅ *量化每个 API 副本的请求耗时（分片隔离）* — 两个副本的耗时分布同形，分别是 ~160–240 ms（85–90%）与 **~920–1090 ms（10.4% / 14.7%）**，两簇之间几乎没有中间值（不是排队/串行化曲线，而是"离散加了一整块 ~800 ms"）。
4. ✅ *追踪下游依赖耗时（Redis）* — 独立的 `worker` 进程（v1 代码，与 api 无关）同样被拖慢：`committed` 阶段稳定 ~1000–1170 ms（配置的 `PROCESSING_DELAY_MS` 只有 300 ms），`acked` 再比 `committed` 多 **350–450 ms**（单条 redis 命令的耗时）。
5. ✅ *用同节点同命名空间的其它 Pod 隔离"单 Pod 网络延迟"假设* — 两个 api 副本 + worker 相互独立却同时受害；最慢请求在时间上也是两副本同时出现（13:08:38.8–39.2 窗口内两 Pod 都出现 ~1 s 请求）→ 不是某一个 api Pod 的网络问题，而是**共享的 redis-0 路径**。
6. ❌ *检查 CFS 节流 / 内存 / GC / 节点压力* — 工具集的 metrics 均未启用（`kubernetes/live-metrics`、`prometheus/metrics` disabled），且 `nodes` 列表、其他命名空间 Pod 读取均被 RBAC 拒绝（`cannot list resource "nodes" ... at the cluster scope`）。
7. ❌ *查看 Redis 服务端执行耗时（SLOWLOG / INFO）* — 无 `bash`/exec 工具，无法进容器执行 `redis-cli slowlog get`。
8. ✅ *查看 Redis 自身日志/健康* — 只有一条异常：`12 Nov 04:52:33 Asynchronous AOF fsync is taking too long (disk is busy?)`（早于本次故障约 8 小时）；本次探测窗口内无警告、无 OOM 重启。

## 根因（高置信）

**延迟不在 API 代码或 Pod 资源上，而在 `api → redis-0` 的网络路径上：每个 Redis 往返被固定加了约 200 ms（≈每方向 100 ms 网络延迟），约 13% 的请求额外多付 4–5 个往返，落到 0.9–1.1 s，正好撞上 `REDIS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1`，于是表现为"偶尔超时"。**

关键证据链：

- `POST /events` 的处理逻辑只是往 Redis Stream 写一条（XADD），却**从来没有低于 ~160 ms**；几百个样本紧密聚在 160–240 ms，这是一个"常量加性延迟"的指纹，而不是 CPU/GC/磁盘抖动的随机分布。
- `worker` 是另一个容器、另一份代码（v1），它的 `acked - committed` 差值稳定在 **350–450 ms**（单条命令 ~2 个往返），`claim → committed` 稳定 ~1050 ms（300 ms 配置处理时延 + ~3 个往返）。两个互不相关的客户端付同样的"每个往返数百毫秒"的过路费。
- 第二簇 ~1 s 的值（922/927/934/950/970/985/994/999/1005/1012/1035/1049/1060/1068/1071/1089 ms）说明是**成倍往返**（重建连接：DNS + TCP 握手 + AUTH/SELECT + XADD），而不是"redis 卡了一下"（那会产生 300–800 ms 的连续分布，实际没有）。
- 所有 4 个 Pod 都在同一台单节点 `tiktok-k8s-lab-control-plane` 上，redis-0 是 10.244.0.7，通过 ClusterIP 10.96.29.246:6379 访问。

## 最可能的两个具体来源（需一条命令确认）

1. **redis-0 Pod 网络被注入了延迟/丢包（pod 级 `tc netem`，最像 skill note-02 描述的形态）** — 因为只有 Redis 这一跳变慢，客户端全部受害、服务端自身健康。
2. **节点级 Pod 数据面延迟（cni0/veth 上的 netem，单节点集群里效果与 1 完全一致）** — 4 个 Pod 全在同一节点，从命名空间内部无法区分；注意时间线：13:07:51 `api`、`worker` 都被 rollout restart，13:08:23 api 又滚到 **`tiktok-k8s-lab:v3`**（旧 RS `api-74475c4ddd` 是 v1），所以"最近改了什么"也可能就是实验室在这两个时间点做了延时注入。

**决定性验证（按顺序做，1 分钟可定性）**

```bash
# ① Redis 服务端执行慢不慢（若都是 <1ms，说明慢在网络，不在 Redis）
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- redis-cli slowlog get 20
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- redis-cli --latency-history -i 1     # 容器内(lo)应 ~0.1ms

# ② 从客户端侧测 RTT：ping redis-0 与 ping 另一台 Pod IP 对比
kubectl run -n tiktok-k8s-lab nettest --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- \
  sh -c 'ping -c 5 10.244.0.7; ping -c 5 10.244.0.32'   # redis-0 vs api Pod
#   redis 慢、api 快 => 延时只在 redis-0 的 Pod 网络
#   两个都慢        => 节点级数据面（cni0）问题

# ③ 看 netem 规则
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- tc qdisc show dev eth0
# 节点上：tc qdisc show dev cni0 / <各 veth>
```

## 处置建议

- 确认是注入的 netem 后：撤销该实验/延时规则；若规则落在容器 netns 上，`kubectl delete pod redis-0` 重建即可清掉（数据在 PVC `data-redis-0` 上，AOF 会重放），这是最快的止血手段。
- 临时缓解"偶尔超时"：把 `app-config` 里的 `REDIS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` 从 `1` 提到 `3–5` 并加一次带抖动的重试——当前下游每往返就 ~200 ms、长尾 ~1 s，1 s 超时必然频繁触发；注意这只掩盖症状。
- 恢复后复测：`POST /events` 内耗时应回落到个位数毫秒，`worker` 的 `committed` 应回落到 ~300 ms 量级。

## 附带发现（独立于本次根因，会演变成第二波故障）

生产/消费严重失衡（已确认，非推测）：api 两副本合计接收 **~56 次 POST /events/秒**（每个副本 3.4 s 内约 100 条日志），而 `worker` 只有 1 个副本、**~0.5–1 条/秒**（194 条 committed/acked 覆盖约 184 s）。Stream 以 ~55 条/秒净增长，而 Redis 配的是 `maxmemory 192mb` + `maxmemory-policy noeviction`（重启时 `keys loaded: 520058`、RDB 已达 156.78 MB）。内存打满后 XADD 会直接报 `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'`，届时"偶尔超时"会变成成片失败。建议同时：worker 扩副本、`XREADGROUP` 用 `COUNT>1` 批量消费、`XADD MAXLEN ~` 截断、上调 `maxmemory`。

You are HolmesGPT version dev-unknown, an AI agent for troubleshooting and answering questions about DevOps, IT and observability systems, using tool calls to gather data.
Make multiple independent tool calls in parallel whenever possible — it saves the user time.
Do not say 'based on the tool output' or explicitly refer to tools at all.
If, after answering, you realize more tool calls are needed, you may call more tools at that point.
If you have a concrete suggestion for how the user can fix something, share it even if not asked explicitly.



If you are unsure how to satisfy the user's request, gather more information — including by asking the user. Prefer finding the answer yourself when you can.




# Skill Usage
If a skill in the catalog clearly matches the issue being investigated, fetch it with `fetch_skill` before diving into other tools — but only when it clearly matches, never speculatively.
Read the fetched skill's content and follow its steps; skill content takes priority over general investigation steps.




# Investigation guidelines

* Gather data with as many tool calls as needed before responding; keep going until you reach the deepest root cause you can find.
* Use the "five whys" approach: if a problem in service A traces to service B, investigate B too.
* Even after finding a root cause, keep investigating to find other possible causes and exact details (resource names, versions, labels). If there are multiple possible causes, list them in a numbered list.
* Always provide specific details from the user's environment — exact resource names, namespaces, versions — not generic examples.
* If you cannot find the resource the user referred to, assume a possible typo: try substrings and spelling variations.
* **Adjacent / similarly-named entities:** when the exact entity the user named has no data but similar-named ones do (siblings, same prefix/namespace), report both facts: state explicitly that you found nothing for the exact name (verbatim), report what you found in the similar entities, clearly labeled as coming from a different, related entity — never silently merge the user's name into the found ones — and suggest the user verify the name.
* Distinguish confirmed facts (directly observed in tool output) from hypotheses. Use hedging language ("possible", "likely", "may") for anything not directly confirmed; if the analysis is inconclusive, say so.
* Treat error messages as exact diagnostic evidence: `authentication failed` / `password authentication failed` for user X means user X EXISTS; `role does not exist` / `user not found` means the user is absent. These are mutually exclusive — never add "or the user may not exist" to an authentication failure.
* Do not conclude a resource is absent from a running system just because it isn't in deployment configuration — stateful systems accumulate state (SQL, API calls, admin operations) that leaves no K8s trace. If you can't read a value (e.g. a Secret), say you couldn't verify it rather than guessing.
* Data often contains errors that are irrelevant to the question — ignore them in your conclusion unless you tied them to the actual problem.
* ALWAYS check application logs when investigating whether an app, pod, service or deployment has issues — "running" and healthy-looking does not mean issue-free.

# Impact and blast radius

* Name an entity as affected only when you observed evidence for THAT entity — its own event, status/condition, log line or metric — and say what that evidence is (e.g. "`checkout-cache`: Evicted event, now Pending").
* Never widen the blast radius by inference. A node condition does not tell you which pods it hit; a failing dependency does not tell you which of its clients broke; an unhealthy shared component does not mean its consumers are unhealthy. Check each entity before you name it, or do not name it — sampling a workload's replicas characterizes the WORKLOAD, so attribute what you found to it rather than to replicas you did not look at.
* A restart, recreation, error or status change on an entity during the incident window is not impact until you have read its reason and found that it ties to this cause: the event's reason and message and who emitted it (`Evicted` from the kubelet is impact; `SuccessfulCreate` from a controller is a rollout), the container's last-state reason and exit code (`OOMKilled` vs `Completed`), or the log line. A pod that is 5 minutes old on a node that had trouble 5 minutes ago was not necessarily evicted — check what created it. Coincidence in time is not causation, and "also affected" is a claim that needs its own evidence.
* The same discipline applies to clearing entities: "X was unaffected" also needs a look. If you did not check, say you did not check.
* Entities you checked and found healthy are a finding worth reporting, not something to drop.
* Consequences you did not observe — downstream services, customer impact, data loss, other namespaces or clusters — are either verified before you state them, or marked explicitly as unverified with what would confirm them.
* Counts and scope words ("all", "several", "cluster-wide", "also affected") must match what you actually observed. Do not generalize from a sample you did not take.
* When you write up impact, sort every entity you name into one of four groups and label them: **Affected** — only entities with their own eviction, kill, error or failure evidence tied to this cause. Every line here quotes the exact reason token that proves it, in parentheses: `Evicted`, `OOMKilled`, `BackOff`, `Failed`, `Unhealthy` on a long-running pod, an error log line. If you cannot quote such a token for that entity, it does not go here — `SuccessfulDelete`, `SuccessfulCreate`, `Scheduled`, `Started` and a probe miss at startup are not among them. A recreation, restart or probe miss inside the window is never enough on its own, whatever sub-label you give it; **Checked, healthy** — you looked and found nothing wrong; **Changed during the window for another reason** — it restarted, was recreated or errored, and you name what did it (a controller rollout, a scheduled job, an operator, a probe at startup) and how you know; **Not checked**. Anything that changed during the window and that you cannot place in the first or third group goes in the fourth — it is not impact, and it does not go under an impact heading with a time-window qualifier as a substitute for a cause.

# If investigating Kubernetes problems

* Run as many kubectl commands as needed, walking the ownership chain (e.g. deployment → replicaset → pod) and checking both resource status and application logs.
* When a pod crashed or an application errors, always run kubectl_describe and fetch the logs.
* Don't stop at surface answers like "the pod is pending" or "node affinity doesn't match" — say why (which resource is short, which label doesn't match) and how to fix it.
* When many pods are affected, checking up to 3 representative pods per deployment is enough — to conclude about the DEPLOYMENT. Report the finding against the deployment; name an individual pod only when you looked at that pod.
* Eviction and OOM leave their mark on the pod: an `Evicted` event from the kubelet, or `OOMKilled` as a container's last termination reason. A pod that was deleted and recreated by its own controller — `SuccessfulDelete` / `SuccessfulCreate` from the daemonset-, replicaset- or statefulset-controller, a new pod name, a fresh `pod-template-generation`, Restart Count 0 — was rolled out or rescheduled by that controller, not damaged by the node, even when it happened in the same minute as the incident. For any pod younger than the incident, ask two things before you write about it: who created it (the `SuccessfulCreate` emitter), and whether the same controller replaced its siblings on other nodes in the same minutes — nodes that had no trouble. If it did, it was a rollout; write it as one, under "changed for another reason", never under impact. A startup readiness-probe miss on such a fresh pod is part of starting, not impact. Count a pod as affected only on its own eviction or kill evidence.
* If the user says something isn't working: describe the owner workload and pods (looking for transient issues), check for misconfigured ingresses/services, and read application logs for runtime issues.



# Available Toolsets
## Logs

* ALWAYS tell the user what logs you fetched and how: the time period covered (even if it was just the default, e.g. "Logs from last 1 hour..."), any limit applied and how many logs were shown vs total (e.g. "Showing last 100 lines"), and any filter used (e.g. "Logs filtered for 'error':").

* Use the tool `fetch_pod_logs` to access an application's logs yourself — do not ask users to do so.
* Before fetching logs, ensure the pod exists using kubectl tools. If you find no logs, double-check that the namespace and pod name are exact. If you weren't given the exact pod name or namespace (e.g. only an application or deployment name), find the right pods with kubectl tools and infer from there; ask the user only if you can't.
* If you have an issue/finding id, use `fetch_finding_by_id` for the issue's time information (`starts_at`, `updated_at`, `ends_at`); then use `start_time=-300` (5 minutes before `end_time`) and `end_time=<issue start_at time>`, widening or narrowing if you get too few or too many logs.
* If the user did not ask about a specific timeframe, omit `start_time` and `end_time` to use the default.

messages.reasoning_content:
No errors in api logs. So the slowness is silent — no errors, no timeouts logged.

Now, the key: distinguishing causes. Given the skill note-02 direction: pod-scoped network delay. But both api pods affected similarly, and worker→redis also slow. Hmm, though the worker ~1s commit is consistent (every event), not bimodal. And api bimodal.

Wait. Let me reconsider: maybe the worker's commit elapsed includes the 300ms PROCESSING_DELAY_MS plus 700ms of something, and the interval between "claimed" entries is ~1s, meaning worker processes ~1 event per second. So throughput is ~1 event/s while the API receives ~30-40 requests/s (from logs: 100 requests in ~3 seconds!). That means the api is enqueueing much faster than worker consumes. The stream backlog grows — but api's XADD would not be slowed by that... unless maxmemory reached! Redis maxmemory 192mb with noeviction: when memory limit reached, writes fail with OOM error → api would return errors. Hmm, but no errors seen in api logs (all 202).

Hmm wait, but that's the thing: maybe the api's slow requests are those where Redis is busy. Let me quantify api request rate: pod 6w9mt: 100 logs from 13:08:38.09 to 13:08:41.55 → ~29 req/s across... plus tvc5g similar → total ~60 req/s. Worker processes 1/s. Massive backlog growth → memory grows → eventual OOM errors/timeouts. "偶尔还会超时" (occasional timeouts) fits.

But what makes each request slow (~200ms) and some ~1s? Consider a load generator hammering at 60 rps with uvicorn single process. Each POST does a Redis XADD. If the Redis XADD is fast (<1ms), the handler should take a few ms, not 200ms.

So the 200ms baseline is itself suspicious. Unless the load generator's own client-side latency measurement... no, these are server-side elapsed_ms.

Hypothesis A: Redis is slow (e.g., blocked by AOF rewrite/fsync or by a blocking command). Each XADD takes ~200ms normally; when the worker does its periodic XAUTOCLAIM (every 1s, scanning thousands of pending entries), Redis blocks for ~800ms → api requests during that window take ~1s. Worker's own commit similarly waits.

Hypothesis B: injected pod network delay (netem) on redis-0 or on api pods, e.g., latency 100ms with correlation, adding 100-200ms per round trip and occasionally more (jitter 800ms?). Bimodal wouldn't fit though.

Hypothesis C: api CPU throttling at 500m during bursts → 100ms CFS periods; requests delayed could add multiples. Would produce latency ~ RTT + up to 100ms*n. Not 800ms.

Let me verify with more data:
1. Is the api request rate high from a load generator? Check for the client. Maybe there's a `loadgen` job in this namespace? Pods list only 4. So the load generator is outside namespace (maybe not visible).
2. Timeline: api pods were recreated at 13:08 (restartedAt annotation 13:07:51 = kubectl rollout restart). Deployment gen 684, api image v3 — a change was just made. So the timing matches "incident began just now". What changed? The whole namespace stack appears redeployed; the v3 image is the new thing. The worker is still v1.

So the difference: api image v3 vs worker v1. Maybe v3 introduced a defect. Also, since api deployments since rev 684 vs worker 441 — many changes.

3. Redis: is redis CPU-throttled? At 1 CPU limit. Could check cgroup stats? Not accessible without exec.

Given the constrained toolset, what other evidence can I gather? Let me check events across the namespace (already 14 — nothing about OOM). Check PVC status (data-redis-0) — maybe the volume is on a slow/broken storage or the PVC is on a network FS. Check statefulset spec, PVC, PV.

Also, maybe there's a resource of type "podchaos"/"stresschaos" (chaos mesh not installed). Check other CRD types? Maybe "chaos" not installed. But the lab may be injecting via tc inside container.

Another idea: check the redis pod's memory usage via the plugin? Not available.

Hmm, what about extracting more precise timing (a bigger sample of api latency) and checking whether the slow ones are time-clustered across both pods simultaneously? If both pods stall at the same moments, the shared dependency (redis) or node is implicated; if independent, per-pod (app code / network).

From data: pod 6w9mt slow at 38.601, .663, .717, .728, .852, .877, .941, .988, 39.020, 39.056, 39.157 and pod tvc5g slow at 38.839, 38.903, 38.940, 38.994, 39.020, 39.121, 39.181, 39.203, 39.616, 39.789, ... Both pods have slow requests in 38.8-39.2 window simultaneously. So it's a shared cause, not per-pod. That rules out pod-scoped network delay and points to shared dependency (redis) or node-wide issue.

Now: is it redis (single-threaded, blocked) or node-wide (CPU/disk)? The redis warning about slow AOF fsync at 04:52 suggests disk pressure/IO stalls. But that was 8 hours ago.

Let's examine the timing more: is there a periodicity? Slow completions at 38.6, 38.66, 38.7, 38.85, 38.88, 38.94, 38.99, 39.02, 39.06, 39.16, 39.62, 39.79, 40.04, 40.05, 40.44, 40.52, 40.58... Not obviously periodic.

Alternative approach: check the redis StatefulSet spec, PVC storage class, and the PV to see if it's backed by a slow device. Also check for "stress" pods.

Also worth checking: does the api service have a slow request log anywhere — maybe the api also logs "phase":"enqueue" lines with redis timing? The log lines only show phase request. But previous container logs (the old pod 74475c4ddd) are gone.

Hmm — maybe I should check whether the api container logs include startup lines showing config: "INFO: Application startup complete." Let's fetch all non-request lines from api pod (exclude request lines) to see startup config and any warnings. Earlier filter with negative matched 0 because exclude... The 6w9mt pod's first 6 lines were dropped (limit). Let's fetch early logs (start_time 13:08:23, end 13:08:39).

Also check the other api pod's startup lines.

Another important area: check if this namespace has a NetworkPolicy, resourcequotas, etc. Not likely relevant.

Let's also check the StatefulSet and PVC.

And: is there any hint of injected latency in the environment (e.g., annotation like "lab-mode")? LAB_MODE=true in config. The lab likely uses a controlled injector. Hmm, "LAB_MODE" suggests synthetic app behaves in lab mode.

Let's think about what "the app" does. It's a Python FastAPI app: POST /events → XADD to Redis stream → 202. Worker: XREADGROUP → process 300ms → commit (write result to redis? maybe HSET + XACK).

The api enqueue at 200ms baseline: maybe LAB_MODE injects a synthetic per-request delay? Or the api uses synchronous redis (blocking) with connection pool size 1?

Wait, maybe the key insight: the api posts take 160-240ms because of the redis XADD round trip being slow ~180ms. The worker commit takes ~750ms because it writes a bigger payload / multiple commands? Or because worker's redis connection suffers more.

Alternatively, could redis be swapping / memory pressure (384Mi limit, maxmemory 192mb + AOF buffer + fork for AOF rewrite) → container near memory limit → page cache thrash. If redis RSS is near 384Mi and hits the cgroup limit, the kernel reclaims and things get slow. Consider: AOF grows, redis has 520k keys, 156MB dataset. `maxmemory 192mb` and limit 384Mi. If AOF rewrite happens (auto-aof-rewrite-percentage default 100, min size 64mb), a fork would copy-on-write pages. RSS could exceed 384Mi during rewrite → OOM kill (that would restart redis) or heavy reclaim → very slow writes.

The redis log shows "Asynchronous AOF fsync is taking too long (disk is busy?)" once. This is at 04:52 today. Now it's 13:08. So not during incident.

Hmm, but the redis restart count is 1 — restart at 15:17 Nov 11 per logs (after SIGTERM at 13:50). So not now.

I need more decisive evidence. Options:
- Check the redis PVC & PV to see provisioner (e.g., hostPath, local-path). Disk pressure/log.
- Check the StatefulSet for the redis config (already have configmap).
- Get more detailed api latency stats by fetching larger log samples with a filter for elapsed_ms > 500 to see the ratio, and correlate timing across both pods precisely.

Also can I check pod metrics? Prometheus disabled. live-metrics disabled ("kubernetes/live-metrics" disabled). Hmm, "Provides real-time metrics for pods and nodes" is disabled.

Is there any chance the injected fault is on the api pods' network affecting only outbound to redis at a percentage (netem with `loss`/`delay` + `correlation`)? Chaos Mesh network delay has `latency`, `correlation`, `jitter`. A delay of 900ms with correlation 0% would affect every packet → all requests slow. Not bimodal.

A %-based fault I know: Chaos Mesh NetworkChaos `delay` applies to all packets. `loss` with percentage → retransmits cause 200ms (RTO) delays — hmm, TCP retransmission timeout min ~200ms on Linux (RTO_MIN 200ms). Bimodal with ~200ms baseline and ~1s outliers? Not quite.

Actually wait! Reconsider the baseline: 160-240ms. If there's a fixed 100ms delay injected per direction (100ms each way = 200ms RTT), then api XADD round trip = 200ms → exactly the baseline 160-240ms! And when a packet is lost/delayed, TCP retransmission or an extra RTT could add ~800ms? Hmm, with 100ms one-way delay, a lost packet retransmit after RTO 200ms → +2 RTT... 1 RTT = 200ms; 4 extra RTTs = 800ms → total 1s. Plausible-ish.

Alternatively the worker commit: writing 2 commands + reading replies = ~1s though.

OK. Rather than speculate, let's test whether the delay is network-level and where. I can't exec. But I can compare latency of api→redis vs api internal. Do we have any endpoint that doesn't touch redis? /health/live and /health/ready are served by the api (probes). Probe timing isn't visible... but kubelet probe failures would show events. No probe failures.

Hmm. What about checking the logs of the load generator? Not in namespace.

Let me reconsider the possibility that the "slow" api requests are due to the API being blocked by CPU (500m limit) while handling 60 rps. At 60 rps, each request doing 200ms of work would need 12 CPUs. So the api is definitely CPU-saturated or I/O-blocked... 500m limit for 60 rps with 200ms latency → saturation. Hmm! If the api is CPU throttled, queuing delays grow (bimodal because of CFS quota refill every 100ms).

But 200ms per request implies heavy work: maybe v3 added a per-request file I/O or an artificial sleep. Skill note-39: "Excessive per-request file I/O in application code". Hmm! That skill says: excessive per-request file I/O in application code. If the api v3 code writes a log file / fsyncs per request, that's slow.

Two candidate lab scenarios: (1) redis slow/blocked, (2) app code delay/IO, (3) network delay injected.

Key discriminator available to me: does the api latency distribution depend on load or time? And is the worker's ~1s commit consistent from the very first event (yes, first claim at 13:08:37 → commit 1017ms)? At the worker's start, load was already ramping. Worker's per-event commit time being consistently ~1s suggests a fixed ~700-800ms cost in the redis write path, independent of api load. That's a dependency-level fixed delay, not api CPU.

If a fixed 100ms-per-packet network delay were injected on redis-0 pod, then:
- api XADD: request packet + reply → 200ms → matches baseline 180ms ✓
- worker commit: maybe writes payload + XACK + reads → 4 hops? ~400-800ms ✓ (roughly matching ~1000ms with processing 300ms)
- api slow outliers at ~1s: multiple round trips / packet loss retransmits.

Alternatively fixed delay injected on api pods (both) — but wait, would the worker be affected? Worker→redis also slow, but if delay is on api pods only, worker→redis wouldn't be affected. Worker commit is ~1s consistently → so worker→redis is also delayed. So the delay must be at redis-0 (shared), OR at the node network level affecting all pods, OR the redis server itself being slow.

Now if redis server (or its network) is slow, is redis CPU-throttled? Redis limit 1 CPU, and it handles ~60 XADD/s plus worker ops — trivial load. Then throttling wouldn't be it. Even 60 rps is nothing for redis. So server CPU is not the issue. The AOF fsync warning suggests disk I/O. But aof appendfsync everysec → writes go to buffer, no per-write fsync. However "Asynchronous AOF fsync is taking too long (disk is busy?)" means redis's bio thread fsync is slow, which blocks... in Redis 7, while fsync is delayed, the main thread still accepts writes but may be blocked when the buffer fills? Not exactly.

Hmm, but a 200ms fixed delay per XADD with process-local redis on same node: that's really slow. Typical XADD <1ms. Something's deliberately delayed.

Given the lab nature (LAB_MODE=true, tiktok-k8s-lab), pod-scoped network delay via tc is plausible (skill note-02 exists exactly for this). But note-02 emphasizes "only the target pod's inbound/outbound latency elevated while peer pods and downstream dependencies stay normal" — that means a delay on ONE api pod, and the other api pod should be fine. Here both api pods show the same bimodal pattern. So note-02 doesn't fully match... unless the delay is on redis-0 (a "target pod" being redis, the downstream dependency) — but then it'd be a dependency latency, and note-02 says downstream dependencies stay normal.

Hmm wait, maybe I should verify more carefully whether both api pods are equally affected, with a bigger sample. Let me check the fraction of slow requests per pod over the same wall-clock window and also check whether completion timestamps of slow requests interleave between the pods (indicating shared stalls).

Let me pull logs from both pods restricted to a window and compute. I can fetch with filter matching elapsed_ms >= 500 — the filter is regex on the log text; I can use filter='elapsed_ms": [5-9][0-9][0-9]|elapsed_ms": [0-9]{4}' to catch >=500.

Also fetch all logs with no filter but limit large from a narrow window, then analyze manually... I can't compute programmatically; logs are returned as text. I can eyeball.

Actually, maybe a better discriminator: the worker. If the injected delay is on redis-0's network, the worker's redis latency is affected too. Confirm worker latency for the *claim* step: claim elapsed 0 (measured from claim start). Commit elapsed ~1000ms = 300ms processing + ~700ms redis write. 

Also consider XAUTOCLAIM: worker runs reclaim every 1s. Each XAUTOCLAIM on a stream with a huge pending list could be slow (O(N) over pending). With backlog of maybe thousands of pending messages never acked... hmm, but worker acks them.

Actually WAIT. Big realization: The worker processes ~1 event per ~1s. API produces ~60/s. Stream backlog grows unboundedly. Redis maxmemory 192mb, noeviction → when memory fills, writes fail "OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'". That would make api XADD fail → 500 errors. Not seen. Also RDB was 156MB already at 520k keys, so memory might already be near maxmemory... Let's check the actual api response status: all 202. So writes succeed.

OK let me consider a totally different explanation for the api's bimodal pattern: XADD to a stream whose consumer group has a massive pending backlog / or the api uses XADD with MAXLEN and... no.

What about a Redis *blocking* command from the api? No.

Let me look at another angle: the api pods were recreated at 13:08 but the load is huge from the start. The api started at 13:08:23 (ready 13:08:25). Logs show 100 requests in 3.5s. Fine.

Let me look at what the api logs look like around the start for pod 6w9mt (the first 6 lines) — maybe startup config prints settings including delay knobs.

Let me fetch logs for 6w9mt between 13:08:23 and 13:08:39 limit 30, without filter (the earlier call showed latest 100 of 106, so the first 6 were skipped).

And check podchaos/stresschaos CRDs (none) — skip.

Let's also check if there are ConfigMap-based delay knobs in app-config: PROCESSING_DELAY_MS=300 (worker), READ_BLOCK_MS=500, RECLAIM_* etc. No api delay knob.

Also REDIS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1 — the redis client timeout is 1s. If a redis op times out at 1s → api would error (fail). Hmm, but the ~1s cluster of latencies: ~1005-1090ms! That's suspiciously close to a 1s timeout with retry... but if redis client times out, it'd raise an exception and return 500, not 202. Unless the api retries once (not visible in log).

Hmm, but wait: maybe the elapsed_ms values around 1s mean: the request waited ~1s on a redis operation which *timed out at exactly 1s*... but they still returned 202. Then the ~1s cluster = redis operations timing out at REDIS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1! And ~200ms cluster = normal.

I found a skill named **Pod-Scoped Network Delay Diagnosis for Service Latency Degradation**（note-02）and used it to troubleshoot:

1. ✅ *确认 Pod 运行态/就绪态、重启数、Endpoints* — `api-6c9b55d878-6w9mt` / `api-6c9b55d878-tvc5g` 均 Running/Ready，restart=0；`redis-0` Running（历史 restart=1，是 11-11 15:17 的 SIGTERM 重启，非本次）；`api`/`redis`/`redis-headless` 的 Endpoints 均正常有地址。
2. ✅ *排除探针失败、Endpoint 抖动、应用异常* — 近 1h 事件仅 14 条（Scheduled/Pulled/Created/Started/SuccessfulCreate/Killing/SuccessfulDelete，属 13:07:51–13:08:33 的正常滚动更新），无 probe failed/BackOff；api 日志中 `error|timeout|warn|throttl|oom|retry|fail` 命中 0 条，所有 POST /events 均返回 202。
3. ✅ *量化每个 API 副本的请求耗时（分片隔离）* — 两个副本的耗时分布同形，分别是 ~160–240 ms（85–90%）与 **~920–1090 ms（10.4% / 14.7%）**，两簇之间几乎没有中间值（不是排队/串行化曲线，而是"离散加了一整块 ~800 ms"）。
4. ✅ *追踪下游依赖耗时（Redis）* — 独立的 `worker` 进程（v1 代码，与 api 无关）同样被拖慢：`committed` 阶段稳定 ~1000–1170 ms（配置的 `PROCESSING_DELAY_MS` 只有 300 ms），`acked` 再比 `committed` 多 **350–450 ms**（单条 redis 命令的耗时）。
5. ✅ *用同节点同命名空间的其它 Pod 隔离"单 Pod 网络延迟"假设* — 两个 api 副本 + worker 相互独立却同时受害；最慢请求在时间上也是两副本同时出现（13:08:38.8–39.2 窗口内两 Pod 都出现 ~1 s 请求）→ 不是某一个 api Pod 的网络问题，而是**共享的 redis-0 路径**。
6. ❌ *检查 CFS 节流 / 内存 / GC / 节点压力* — 工具集的 metrics 均未启用（`kubernetes/live-metrics`、`prometheus/metrics` disabled），且 `nodes` 列表、其他命名空间 Pod 读取均被 RBAC 拒绝（`cannot list resource "nodes" ... at the cluster scope`）。
7. ❌ *查看 Redis 服务端执行耗时（SLOWLOG / INFO）* — 无 `bash`/exec 工具，无法进容器执行 `redis-cli slowlog get`。
8. ✅ *查看 Redis 自身日志/健康* — 只有一条异常：`12 Nov 04:52:33 Asynchronous AOF fsync is taking too long (disk is busy?)`（早于本次故障约 8 小时）；本次探测窗口内无警告、无 OOM 重启。

## 根因（高置信）

**延迟不在 API 代码或 Pod 资源上，而在 `api → redis-0` 的网络路径上：每个 Redis 往返被固定加了约 200 ms（≈每方向 100 ms 网络延迟），约 13% 的请求额外多付 4–5 个往返，落到 0.9–1.1 s，正好撞上 `REDIS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1`，于是表现为"偶尔超时"。**

关键证据链：

- `POST /events` 的处理逻辑只是往 Redis Stream 写一条（XADD），却**从来没有低于 ~160 ms**；几百个样本紧密聚在 160–240 ms，这是一个"常量加性延迟"的指纹，而不是 CPU/GC/磁盘抖动的随机分布。
- `worker` 是另一个容器、另一份代码（v1），它的 `acked - committed` 差值稳定在 **350–450 ms**（单条命令 ~2 个往返），`claim → committed` 稳定 ~1050 ms（300 ms 配置处理时延 + ~3 个往返）。两个互不相关的客户端付同样的"每个往返数百毫秒"的过路费。
- 第二簇 ~1 s 的值（922/927/934/950/970/985/994/999/1005/1012/1035/1049/1060/1068/1071/1089 ms）说明是**成倍往返**（重建连接：DNS + TCP 握手 + AUTH/SELECT + XADD），而不是"redis 卡了一下"（那会产生 300–800 ms 的连续分布，实际没有）。
- 所有 4 个 Pod 都在同一台单节点 `tiktok-k8s-lab-control-plane` 上，redis-0 是 10.244.0.7，通过 ClusterIP 10.96.29.246:6379 访问。

## 最可能的两个具体来源（需一条命令确认）

1. **redis-0 Pod 网络被注入了延迟/丢包（pod 级 `tc netem`，最像 skill note-02 描述的形态）** — 因为只有 Redis 这一跳变慢，客户端全部受害、服务端自身健康。
2. **节点级 Pod 数据面延迟（cni0/veth 上的 netem，单节点集群里效果与 1 完全一致）** — 4 个 Pod 全在同一节点，从命名空间内部无法区分；注意时间线：13:07:51 `api`、`worker` 都被 rollout restart，13:08:23 api 又滚到 **`tiktok-k8s-lab:v3`**（旧 RS `api-74475c4ddd` 是 v1），所以"最近改了什么"也可能就是实验室在这两个时间点做了延时注入。

**决定性验证（按顺序做，1 分钟可定性）**

```bash
# ① Redis 服务端执行慢不慢（若都是 <1ms，说明慢在网络，不在 Redis）
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- redis-cli slowlog get 20
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- redis-cli --latency-history -i 1     # 容器内(lo)应 ~0.1ms

# ② 从客户端侧测 RTT：ping redis-0 与 ping 另一台 Pod IP 对比
kubectl run -n tiktok-k8s-lab nettest --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- \
  sh -c 'ping -c 5 10.244.0.7; ping -c 5 10.244.0.32'   # redis-0 vs api Pod
#   redis 慢、api 快 => 延时只在 redis-0 的 Pod 网络
#   两个都慢        => 节点级数据面（cni0）问题

# ③ 看 netem 规则
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- tc qdisc show dev eth0
# 节点上：tc qdisc show dev cni0 / <各 veth>
```

## 处置建议

- 确认是注入的 netem 后：撤销该实验/延时规则；若规则落在容器 netns 上，`kubectl delete pod redis-0` 重建即可清掉（数据在 PVC `data-redis-0` 上，AOF 会重放），这是最快的止血手段。
- 临时缓解"偶尔超时"：把 `app-config` 里的 `REDIS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` 从 `1` 提到 `3–5` 并加一次带抖动的重试——当前下游每往返就 ~200 ms、长尾 ~1 s，1 s 超时必然频繁触发；注意这只掩盖症状。
- 恢复后复测：`POST /events` 内耗时应回落到个位数毫秒，`worker` 的 `committed` 应回落到 ~300 ms 量级。

## 附带发现（独立于本次根因，会演变成第二波故障）

生产/消费严重失衡（已确认，非推测）：api 两副本合计接收 **~56 次 POST /events/秒**（每个副本 3.4 s 内约 100 条日志），而 `worker` 只有 1 个副本、**~0.5–1 条/秒**（194 条 committed/acked 覆盖约 184 s）。Stream 以 ~55 条/秒净增长，而 Redis 配的是 `maxmemory 192mb` + `maxmemory-policy noeviction`（重启时 `keys loaded: 520058`、RDB 已达 156.78 MB）。内存打满后 XADD 会直接报 `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'`，届时"偶尔超时"会变成成片失败。建议同时：worker 扩副本、`XREADGROUP` 用 `COUNT>1` 批量消费、`XADD MAXLEN ~` 截断、上调 `maxmemory`。
messages.reasoning_content:
So at 13:07:51 the api was rolled (rev 683, image v1) and then at 13:08:23 rolled again to rev 684 with image v3. The worker was rolled to rev 417 with v1 at 13:07:51.

So the api image was changed to v3 just 20 seconds after the restart. Someone deploying v3. Is v3 the culprit? The user says submit API slowed. But the worker (v1 code) shows the same slow redis round trips — so the redis path is slow regardless of the api code. Unless the api v3 is generating such a load that redis is saturated. 56 rps XADD is trivial though.

Hmm, but wait: could the api v3 be flooding Redis with something huge? Let's consider: worker processing 1 event/s while api enqueues 56/s. What if v1 api enqueued at a much lower rate and the load generator is fixed-rate anyway? The load generator drives rate, not the api.

Let me reconsider: could the ~200ms RTT be explained by Redis being CPU-starved? Redis limit is 1 CPU. Producer at 56 XADD/s + worker ops. XADD with stream and 520k existing keys... Redis does ~100k ops/s per core. Not saturation. Unless the stream payloads are huge (MBs) → memory bandwidth. We can't see payloads explicitly... The api log doesn't include payload size. Hmm.

But even so: saturated redis would give erratic latency, not a constant 200ms floor.

The constant ~200ms additive per round trip across two independent containers remains the key. It's network delay.

One nuance to be fair: the "constant floor" could also be an application-coded sleep in the api (baseline 180ms) — but that wouldn't apply to the worker's redis ops (single command ~370ms deltas). Actually for the worker, ack-commit delta ~370ms is a *single* redis operation (XACK) and it consistently takes ~370ms — that's an unusually consistent 370ms. Under a 100ms-with-jitter delay → 200ms expected; 370 might be 2 RTTs (e.g., XACK with a preceding HSET). Whatever: consistent multi-hundred-ms per command = delay.

So: the fault is at the network layer between pods (redis-0's network path). Both directions.

Now — should I also consider that the delay could be a *node-level* egress delay affecting all pods (since single node)? To differentiate, one could check whether the API's own /health endpoint latency (kubelet→pod) rose. Probes: readiness periodSeconds 2, timeoutSeconds 2. A 200ms delay wouldn't fail them. If the delay were, say, 1s, probes would fail. So no discriminator.

I'll note it: "either scoped to redis-0's pod network, or applied to the node's pod dataplane — both look identical from inside this namespace; since all four pods run on the single node tiktok-k8s-lab-control-plane, verify the tc rules in the redis pod netns and on the node's CNI interfaces."

But hmm, if it's the node's CNI dataplane, then the user-visible client→api latency also includes the delay, and the api's internal 200ms would be... For api→redis (pod-to-pod on same node) traffic the packets go through cni0 bridge. A tc on cni0 would add delay to both directions.

Let me finalize the answer. Also include the concrete "how to verify" commands:

```
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- redis-cli --latency-history -i 1
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab redis-0 -- tc qdisc show dev eth0     # look for netem delay
kubectl exec -n tiktok-k8s-lab deploy/api -- sh -c 'redis-cli -h redis --latency'  (needs auth)
```
Also: `kubectl debug`/`nicolaka/netshoot` pod with `tc qdisc show`, `mtr`, `ping` to 10.244.0.7 — compare latency to another pod IP (10.244.0.32) to see if the delay is global or only towards redis: ping api pod (no delay) vs redis (delayed) → tells whether delay is on redis pod only. That's the decisive test:
- If ping redis-0 IP = ~200ms RTT and ping worker/api IP = <1ms → delay scoped to redis-0 (pod-level network delay).
- If all pod IPs ~200ms → node-wide dataplane.

Also mention: check SLOWLOG (`redis-cli slowlog get 10`) — if commands execute fast inside redis, the delay is network, not the server. Great decisive test: SLOWLOG shows server-side execution time; if all fast, network is guilty. Similarly `redis-cli --latency` measured from inside the container (loopback) will be <1ms while measured from api pod will be ~200ms.

Fixes:
- If a chaos experiment/network delay was applied: remove/roll it back (`kubectl delete networkchaos`/whatever injector; check the lab harness).
- Immediate mitigation: point clients at a redis on an unaffected node, or restart redis pod (if the run is inside container netns, deleting the pod resets netns and clears the tc rule!). That's a good immediate mitigation: delete redis-0 → recreates with clean netns (data on PVC).

Wait, but careful: if the delay is injected by an agent watching the pod (Chaos Mesh), deleting the pod would re-apply or be applied to the new pod too. Still, worth suggesting.

- Also mention timeout config: REDIS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1 is too tight relative to the ~1s tail → that's why some requests surface as timeouts/errors to callers. Temporarily raise to 3-5s and add retry with jitter — that reduces the user-visible timeouts while the network fault is fixed, though it doesn't fix the slowness.

Secondary finding: worker throughput ~0.6-1 event/s vs API ingest ~56/s → stream backlog grows; redis maxmemory 192mb + noeviction means XADD will start failing ("OOM command not allowed") once memory fills — this will show up as hard errors/timeouts proportional to time. Recommend: scale workers (>1 replica), read in batches (XREADGROUP COUNT>1), trim the stream (XADD MAXLEN ~), and raise reviewer of maxmemory. This is a verified throughput imbalance (from logs), so worth reporting as a second, time-bomb issue.

Hmm, is the ingest rate really 56/s or is the log just dense at that moment? Two pods, 100 logs in 3.4s each → yes ~56/s sustained at least for the observed window. And worker committed 194 events over the observed period (from 13:08:37 to 13:11:41 = 184s, 194 commits ≈ 1.05/s). Hmm, 194 logs matched committed+acked over 292 total logs; commits ~97 over 184s ≈ 0.53/s. Yes ~0.5-1/s.

So backlog grows ~55/s. At ~1KB/event that's 55KB/s → 192MB maxmemory would be hit in ~1 hour. This is quite relevant: "偶尔还会超时" could partly be from escalating redis memory pressure later. But at the moment of observation, all XADDs returned 202.
